  1           Pursuant to Civil Local Rules 6-2 and 7-11 of the Northern District of California, Plaintiff
 2   Wade Benton (“Plaintiff”) and Defendant CiVi Biopharma Holdings, Inc. (“CiVi” or
 3   “Defendant”) (collectively, the "Parties"), by and through their respective counsel of record,
 4   hereby submit this Joint Stipulated Request for an Order extending Defendant’s time to answer
 5   Plaintiff’s Second Amended Complaint.
 6           WHEREAS, Plaintiff filed his original Complaint on January 31, 2025 (ECF No. 1);
 7           WHEREAS, on August 8, 2025, Plaintiff filed his First Amended Complaint in this
 8   action, asserting claims against Defendants (ECF No. 13);

15   to resolve this matter in its entirety.
16           WHEREAS, to allow adequate time to finalize responsive pleadings while conducting
17   settlement discussions, the Parties have agreed to a two-week extension of Defendant's deadline
18   to answer, moving it from August 24, 2026, to September 7, 2026.
19           NOW THEREFORE, the parties hereby stipulate that defendant CiVi may file its answer
20   on or before September 7, 2026.

                                   9

                                  10        CIVI BIOPHARMA HOLDINGS, INC., et
                                            al.,                                             Re: ECF Nos. 76, 77
                                  11                    Defendants.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           Before the Court are motions to dismiss filed by Defendants CiVi Biopharma Holdings,

                                  14   Inc. and BTG International, Inc. ECF Nos. 76, 77. The Court will grant BTG’s motion and deny

                                  15   CiVi’s motion.

                                  16   I.      BACKGROUND

                                  17           The following facts are taken from the second amended complaint (“SAC”). Plaintiff

                                  18   Wade Benton founded Eicos Sciences, Inc. with Kevin Christal in 2016. ECF No. 73 ¶ 21. Eicos

                                  19   was founded to develop new uses for an orphan drug known as iloprost. Id. Because iloprost is a

                                  20   vasodilator, a drug that opens blood vessels and increases bloodflow, Eicos intended to use it to

                                  21   treat diseases and injuries characterized by restricted circulation and fibrosis. Id. ¶¶ 23, 28.

                                  22            In 2018, Benton, along with Christal and the other Eicos stockholders (“the Eicos

                                  23   Sellers”), entered into a Stock Purchase Agreement (“SPA”) with CiVi. Id. ¶ 29. Under the SPA,

                                  24   CiVi purchased all shares of Eicos. Id. Concomitantly, Benton and the Eicos stockholders

                                  25   entered into the Sellers’ Representative Agreement (“SRA”), making Benton the Sellers’

                                  26   Representative and vesting Benton with certain rights and responsibilities pertaining to the sale of

                                  27   Eicos and the development and marketing of iloprost. Id. ¶ 30.

                                  28           As consideration for the purchase of Eicos, CiVi agreed to pay Benton, as Sellers’
                                        Case 4:25-cv-01000-JST           Document 103          Filed 08/10/26    Page 2 of 13




                                   1   Representative: (1) a $2,000,000.00 “Base Purchase Price” within 60 days of the FDA’s approval

                                   2   of a New Drug Application (“NDA”) of an Eicos-developed drug containing or derived from

                                   3   iloprost for use in the United States to treat systemic sclerosis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, or

                                   4   idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; and (2) “Milestone Payments” that would become due as Eicos-

                                   5   developed drugs met certain sales targets. Id. ¶ 31. Benton and Christal also agreed to become

                                   6   “Key Employees” of Eicos and/or CiVi after the purchase and at least until the FDA approved an

                                   7   Eicos-developed drug containing or derived from iloprost. Id. ¶ 35. If either left Eicos or CiVi

                                   8   prematurely, they would forfeit 50% of any Milestone Payments. Id.

                                   9          Experiencing difficulties securing FDA approval for an iloprost-derived drug to treat

                                  10   systemic sclerosis, Benton and Christal decided to target frostbite. Id. ¶ 37. After receiving

                                  11   positive initial feedback from the FDA about the use of iloprost to treat frostbite, Benton, as the

                                  12   Sellers’ Representative, and CiVi executed an Amendment Agreement (“the Amendment”) adding
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   frostbite to the list of treated conditions that would trigger CiVi’s obligation to pay the Base

                                  14   Purchase Price and Milestone Payments. Id. ¶¶ 40–41. While negotiating the Agreement, Benton

                                  15   and Christal informed CiVi that they would not continue working to develop iloprost unless CiVi

                                  16   made the commitments in the Amendment. Id. ¶ 42.

                                  17          Upon signing the Amendment, Benton and Christal continued to work on iloprost for

                                  18   Eicos/CiVi, securing FDA priority review for an iloprost-derived frostbite treatment in early 2023.

                                  19   Id. ¶ 43. The FDA approved Eicos’s NDA for an iloprost-derived frostbite treatment on February

                                  20   13, 2024, under the brand name Aurlumyn. Id. ¶ 45. As a result of the FDA’s approval of

                                  21   Aurlumyn, the Base Purchase Price became due on April 13, 2024 under the SPA and the

                                  22   Amendment. Id. ¶¶ 50–52. Benton has since repeatedly demanded that CiVi pay the Base

                                  23   Purchase Price, including in writing. Id. ¶ 53. Despite Benton’s repeated demands, CiVi has

                                  24   refused to pay the Base Purchase Price or provide assurances that it will pay any Milestone

                                  25   Payments. Id. ¶¶ 54–55.

                                  26          On October 21, 2024, BTG’s parent corporation, SERB SAS, announced that it had

                                  27   acquired the rights to Aurlumyn from CiVi (“the Assignment”). Id. ¶ 60. In the Asset Purchase

                                  28   Agreement (“APA”) between CiVi and BTG, the SPA and the Amendment are listed as “excluded
                                                                                          2
                                        Case 4:25-cv-01000-JST            Document 103           Filed 08/10/26     Page 3 of 13




                                   1   liabilities” which CiVi will retain and remain responsible for. Id.¶ 62. The Assignment also

                                   2   required CiVi to indemnify BTG against claims arising out of the SPA or any other excluded

                                   3   liabilities. Id. ¶ 66. The APA, “in the form available to Benton, does not describe payments

                                   4   sufficient for CiVi to perform its obligations under the SPA.” Id. ¶ 64.

                                  15   III.    LEGAL STANDARD

                                  16           A.      Rule 12(b)(2)

                                  17           Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(2), the court must dismiss an action if it does not

                                  18   have personal jurisdiction over the defendant. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(2). “In opposition to a

                                  19   defendant’s motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, the plaintiff bears the burden of

                                  20   establishing that jurisdiction is proper.” Boschetto v. Hansing, 539 F.3d 1011, 1015 (9th Cir. 2008).

                                  21   Where “the motion is based on written materials rather than an evidentiary hearing, ‘the plaintiff need

                                  22   only make a prima facie showing of jurisdictional facts.’” Schwarzenegger v. Fred Martin Motor Co.,

                                  23   374 F.3d 797, 800 (9th Cir. 2004) (quoting Sher v. Johnson, 911 F.2d 1357, 1361 (9th Cir. 1990)).

                                  24   “Although the plaintiff cannot simply rest on the bare allegations of its complaint, uncontroverted

                                  25   allegations in the complaint must be taken as true. Conflicts between parties over statements contained

                                  26   in affidavits must be resolved in the plaintiff’s favor.” Id. (internal quotation marks and citations

                                  27   omitted).

                                  28
                                                                                            3

                                   1           “Federal courts ordinarily follow state law in determining the bounds of their jurisdiction over

                                   2   persons.” Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117, 125 (2014). “California’s long-arm statute allows

                                   3   the exercise of personal jurisdiction to the full extent permissible under the U.S. Constitution.” Id.

                                   4   Because the applicable state “statute is coextensive with federal due process requirements, the

                                   5   jurisdictional analyses under state law and federal due process are the same.” Schwarzenegger, 374

                                   6   F.3d at 800–01.

                                   7           Due process permits a court to exercise personal jurisdiction over a defendant only when “the

                                   8   defendant has sufficient minimum contacts with the forum state such that the maintenance of the suit

                                   9   does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.” Impossible Foods Inc. v.

                                  10   Impossible X LLC, 80 F.4th 1079, 1086 (9th Cir. 2023) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).

                                  11   “The strength of contacts required depends on which of the two categories of personal jurisdiction a

                                  12   litigant invokes: specific jurisdiction or general jurisdiction.” Ranza v. Nike, Inc., 793 F.3d 1059, 1068
Northern District of California

                                  13   (9th Cir. 2015). For the court to exercise specific jurisdiction, the lawsuit must arise out of or relate to

                                  14   the defendant’s contacts with the forum. Id. In other words, there must be “an affiliation between the

                                  15   forum and the underlying controversy, principally, [an] activity or an occurrence that takes place in the

                                  16   forum state and is therefore subject to the state’s regulation.” Id. (quoting Goodyear Dunlop Tires

                                  17   Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915, 919 (2011)).

                                  18           B.      Rule 12(b)(6)

                                  19           A complaint must contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the

                                  20   pleader is entitled to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2). “Dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) is

                                  21   appropriate only where the complaint lacks a cognizable legal theory or sufficient facts to support

                                  22   a cognizable legal theory.” Mendiondo v. Centinela Hosp. Med. Ctr., 521 F.3d 1097, 1104 (9th

                                  23   Cir. 2008). A complaint need not contain detailed factual allegations, but facts pleaded by a

                                  24   plaintiff “must be enough to raise a right to relief above the speculative level.” Bell Atl. Corp. v.

                                  25   Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). “To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain

                                  26   sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”

                                  27   Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted). “A

                                  28   claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw
                                                                                            4

                                  27   BTG’s motion to dismiss. Because Plaintiff has had an opportunity to amend his allegations as to

                                  28   personal jurisdiction over BTG, further leave to amend would be futile and the complaint is
